title: Make your offer easier to understand.
content:
We work through page structure, responsive layouts, content hierarchy, and review rounds with you. The proposal states whether the engagement includes implementation, a design handoff, or both.
Current-site and conversion review: Inventory current pages and content, top landing pages, Search Console queries, analytics, mobile navigation, forms and CTA visibility. Trace CRM/inquiry delivery and form friction; review proof and pricing context before deciding which templates need redesign.
Intent and navigation map: Map the buyer questions to service pages, related guidance and proof. Preserve useful URLs and content; identify navigation labels or repeated sections that make the next step hard to find.
Wireframes for key tasks: Sketch the service answer, trust evidence, mobile CTA and inquiry path. Check focus order, heading structure and what a user must provide before submitting a form. A short form still needs enough context for follow-up.
Content and evidence review: Work with approved service facts, images and portfolio contributions. Identify missing buyer answers and unsupported claims instead of filling space with reassurance. You approve business facts and supplied assets.
Responsive design and handoff: Apply the established brand to agreed templates, mobile layouts and interaction states. Review the primary journey, hand off components and content requirements, and state whether implementation is included.
Which landing pages receive relevant search visits?
Can a new visitor identify the service, area and next step?
Does proof explain the actual contribution without claiming an unverified outcome?
Where does the mobile form create friction?
Is the main issue design, content or a failed delivery integration?
When customers cannot find the right service or know what to do next, a redesign needs more than a new visual style. We clarify page structure, content hierarchy, mobile navigation, and inquiry paths for your audience.
Deliverables:
Discovery notes, page inventory, and a proposed information structure
Wireframes and responsive page designs for agreed templates
Design review, implementation handoff, and agreed accessibility and mobile checks
Scope:
We agree on pages, templates, revisions, and whether development is included. Photography, brand identity creation, ongoing copywriting, and extensive content migration require their own scope. You approve factual claims and supply assets you have permission to use.
Pricing basis:
Web package totals below cover the published package scope. A design-only engagement or larger redesign is quoted by templates, content needs, implementation work, and review rounds.
What we look for in a service website
A clear H1 and understandable service offer.
An accurate location or service area, without invented offices.
Trust evidence connected to the offer, with portfolio roles attributed accurately.
A visible mobile CTA, easy navigation and a low-friction form.
Useful pricing context and clear scope boundaries.
Consent-aware analytics and search-friendly content.
A journey map before new visuals
For a service-business redesign, map search query → landing page → service explanation → relevant proof → inquiry. Record the intended next action and how delivery will be verified. This is a planning artifact, not a claim of conversion lift.
Keep working content and familiar interactions when they serve that journey. A redesign may be unnecessary if the main problem is broken form delivery, unclear pricing or one missing service answer.
Can you redesign without replacing everything? We review the existing structure and identify the pages, navigation, and interactions that need attention.
Is development included? The proposal states whether the work includes implementation, a design handoff, or both.
Can you help organize our content? Yes. We can map key messages and page structure. Content production and migration volumes are agreed separately.
Will the design work on phones? Responsive layouts and checks of agreed mobile journeys form part of the design scope.
Does a redesign guarantee more inquiries? No. We can improve clarity and make inquiry paths measurable, then evaluate results with real visitors.
David Dare MD portfolio: Treatment information hierarchy and appointment pathways; contribution details are described in the portfolio. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/case-studies/daremd/

title: A website or business app your team can use.
content:
From a service website to a scoped business application, we agree on users, data, permissions, content, and integrations before selecting an implementation approach.
Map the workflow and dependencies: Define users, roles, data ownership, approved actions and acceptance checks. Review the existing CMS, migration needs, licensing and external API limits before choosing a stack.
Make architecture decisions explicit: Choose static generation, server rendering or an authenticated application by content freshness and access requirements. Separate CMS content from transactional data and define integration timeouts, retries and idempotent actions.
Build and verify the critical path: Implement the agreed responsive pages, CMS or application features, integrations and inquiry states. Test successful and failed submissions, permission boundaries, API timeouts and duplicate events, not just the happy path.
Release and hand off: Document access, deployment, cache invalidation, rollback and routine operations. Review core workflows with the client and distinguish launch acceptance from ongoing hosting, support and feature work.
Does the page need server-side rendering?
Does it benefit from static generation?
Does the system need authentication?
Who owns the data?
What happens if an API fails?
What actions must be idempotent?
How should retries work?
What happens after a failed form submission?
What data belongs in the CMS?
What belongs in an application database?
If your website hides your services, forms lose inquiries, or staff copy information between tools, start with the workflow. We build marketing websites, portals, and business applications around the tasks your customers and team need to complete.
Deliverables:
A written scope, page or workflow map, and integration requirements
Responsive implementation, agreed CMS or application features, and inquiry paths
Testing of core workflows, launch checklist, and handoff documentation
Scope:
A brochure website package does not include an unlimited custom application. Authentication, complex data migration, external APIs, hosting, software licenses, and ongoing operations are scoped separately. You provide access, approved content, and feedback; we agree on acceptance checks before development.
Pricing basis:
Published Web packages provide a starting point for websites. Application pricing depends on roles, workflows, data, integrations, and testing requirements. Confirm what is included in a written proposal.
Failure planning is part of the workflow
CRM unavailable: Show a truthful delivery state, retain only approved retry data and offer a Contact fallback.
API timeout: Set timeout and retry limits; explain whether the user can safely try again.
Duplicate webhook: Use an idempotency key or processed-event record to avoid repeating an action.
Failed form notification: Do not show or record a delivered lead until the server confirms delivery; provide a recoverable retry.
Deployment failure: Define release checks, rollback ownership and the previous working version.
Stale cache: Agree which content can be cached and how publishing invalidates it.
Authentication/session expiry: Require reauthentication where needed and preserve only appropriate draft state.
Rendering and data tradeoffs
A stable service page may suit static generation. Frequently changing or personalized data may require server rendering or a protected application request. Choose by freshness, access control and operating cost rather than adding a server to every page.
Keep editorial content in the CMS when nontechnical staff need publishing control. Transactional records and permissioned workflow state usually need an application database with validation, access rules and an agreed retention policy.
Can you build a business application instead of a marketing site? Yes. We first define users, permissions, data, workflows, and integrations, then quote the application scope separately from a website package.
Can we keep our existing CMS? We review its access, templates, data, and integration limits before recommending an extension or migration.
How long will development take? The schedule depends on the approved scope, content readiness, integrations, and review cycles. Milestones are agreed after discovery.
Will the site generate leads automatically? We can implement clear inquiry paths and measurement. Traffic, visitor fit, and commercial results require ongoing review; no lead volume is guaranteed.
Do you work outside Long Island? KDH is based in Freeport, serves Long Island and NYC, and can deliver projects remotely.
Who owns the code and accounts? The proposal defines code ownership, repository access and handoff. Third-party software keeps its own license terms; agree on hosting, CMS and integration account ownership before work starts.
IIN contribution overview: Professional engineering contributions to enrollment workflows; not presented as a verified KDH agency engagement. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/case-studies/iin/

title: An architecture and implementation scope for your office.
content:
KDH plans business network architecture for Long Island and NYC offices: routing, switching, wireless placement, segmentation and failover. We start with users, devices, applications, the building and reusable equipment, then define configuration and acceptance checks.
Inventory devices and physical constraints: Record user/device counts, floor plans, cable paths, PoE needs, existing equipment and ISP options. Identify voice, guest and IoT systems, remote management needs and latency-sensitive applications.
Design routing, switching and segmentation: Define VLANs, addressing, DHCP/DNS ownership and permitted traffic paths. Size switch ports, uplinks and PoE budgets. Segmentation needs routing/firewall rules and verification; VLAN numbers alone do not enforce isolation.
Plan Wi-Fi placement and capacity: Place access points using building constraints and expected client density. Review channel use and roaming paths. Reuse compatible equipment where it meets requirements; replacement is a scope decision supported by access, support status and capacity findings.
Choose redundancy and failover deliberately: Compare a second ISP, backup gateway and switch redundancy with the cost of an outage. Dual connections may share a physical failure point. Load balancing distributes selected traffic and is not the same as preserving every active session during failover.
Configure, verify and hand off: Agree on installation/cabling responsibilities, a maintenance window and rollback plan. Test approved inter-VLAN paths, guest isolation, wireless locations and ISP failover where included. Deliver device/configuration records and known dependencies.
How many users and devices need access?
Which applications are latency-sensitive?
Is guest access required?
Is failover required, and what interruption can the business tolerate?
Are voice systems present?
Is remote management needed?
Are IoT devices present?
What segmentation and permitted paths are necessary?
What ISP options exist?
What equipment can be reused?
Moves, office expansion, mixed guest/staff access and recurring capacity issues call for a design review. Replacing a router alone may not address cable, coverage or ISP constraints.
Deliverables:
Device inventory, topology and addressing/VLAN plan
Access-point placement and capacity assumptions
Routing/firewall path requirements and failover choices
Configuration, validation and handoff checklist with implementation responsibilities
Scope:
The proposal distinguishes planning, equipment procurement, configuration, physical installation and cabling. Replacement hardware, ISP fees, electrical work and specialist cybersecurity/SOC services are separate unless included. A network design does not guarantee zero downtime, certification or regulatory compliance.
Pricing basis:
Published Network setup ranges are $2,000–$3,500, $5,000–$8,000 and $10,000–$15,000+ for their stated scopes. Device count, sites, cabling, wireless coverage, PoE, redundancy and installation windows determine the proposal. Monthly support is separate.
Example small-business network architecture
This is an example only. Actual segmentation depends on devices, business requirements, risk, building layout and existing systems. Decide permitted paths and management access explicitly; do not copy the example as a one-size-fits-all installation.
Internet / ISP → Firewall / Gateway → Core switch
Core switch → VLAN 10 — Staff
Core switch → VLAN 20 — Voice
Core switch → VLAN 30 — Guest
Core switch → VLAN 40 — IoT
Wireless access points connect through the switching infrastructure.
Reuse, redundancy and capacity tradeoffs
Keeping a supported switch may preserve budget for coverage or cabling. A second uplink may add capacity while leaving a single gateway failure point. Choose the dependency that matters to the business task, then agree on a test that checks the design assumption.
Can existing equipment be reused? We check firmware support, management access, capacity, ports and PoE against the proposed design before recommending reuse or replacement.
Does every office need four VLANs? No. The example separates staff, voice, guest and IoT traffic; actual segmentation depends on devices, risk and business requirements.
Does a second ISP prevent all outages? No. Providers may share physical infrastructure, and gateways, power or cabling can remain failure points. Define and test the intended failover.
Is cabling included? Only where the written project scope includes it. Planning, equipment and installation responsibilities must be confirmed separately.
Example small-business architecture: An illustrative staff/voice/guest/IoT segmentation artifact, not a customer deployment or a mandatory design. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/guides/business-network-review/#network-example

title: A baseline and a change record you can compare.
content:
KDH reviews business Wi-Fi and network performance for Long Island and NYC offices using baseline measurements, coverage checks and post-change tests. We separate radio coverage, client capacity, switching and ISP limitations before recommending configuration or hardware changes.
Baseline measurement: Record the application, device, location, time and client load. Compare wired throughput and latency with wireless results so an upstream ISP or switch limitation is not mistaken for weak Wi-Fi.
Coverage and RF review: Review RSSI, SNR and interference at working locations, not just beside the access point. Check placement, walls, neighboring networks and roaming behavior using representative client devices.
Channel and capacity analysis: Inspect channel utilization, frequency/channel choices and client density. More access points or wider channels can increase contention; evaluate placement and capacity rather than changing every setting at once.
Controlled configuration changes: Agree on a window, preserve the existing configuration and adjust the suspected cause. This may involve channels, power, access-point placement, traffic priorities or upstream configuration. Hardware changes need their own approval.
Post-change testing and documentation: Repeat throughput, packet loss, latency and jitter tests at comparable locations and load. Verify the original application and roaming path, then document changes, measured differences and remaining limits. Ongoing monitoring needs an explicit support scope.
Does the same task fail over a wired connection?
Are RSSI and SNR adequate where users work?
Is contention driven by channels, interference or client density?
Does the call fail while roaming between access points?
Can tuning solve the issue, or does coverage require a design change?
Slow calls, interrupted roaming and inconsistent file transfers can have different causes. The review focuses on the affected locations and business applications rather than promising maximum speed everywhere.
Deliverables:
Baseline results with device, location and load assumptions
Coverage/RF, channel and capacity findings
Approved configuration changes and post-change tests
Documentation of measured differences, remaining constraints and recommendations
Scope:
An optimization review is not a new cabling installation or unlimited hardware rollout. ISP capacity, building construction, client capabilities and equipment limits affect results. Security/SOC work and ongoing monitoring need separate scope. No minimum speed, universal coverage or uninterrupted roaming is guaranteed.
Pricing basis:
Scope depends on floor area, sites, client density, equipment access, testing windows and whether an on-site review is needed. Published Network setup ranges are package context, not a fixed optimization fee. Hardware, ISP upgrades, cabling and recurring support are separate unless included.
Why speed tests are not enough
A speed test measures one path at one moment. Wi-Fi can still be poor because of weak signal, interference, channel contention, client density, roaming behavior or upstream configuration. Compare the actual business task with a wired baseline and repeat at the locations where the issue occurs.
Read the network measurements
RSSI: Received signal level at a client location; useful for comparing coverage.
SNR: Signal-to-noise ratio; a strong signal can still compete with noise.
Channel utilization: How busy shared airtime is; high contention can reduce useful capacity.
Packet loss: Packets that do not arrive; compare wireless and upstream paths.
Latency: Round-trip delay to a defined destination.
Throughput: Useful transferred data per unit time; depends on the tested path and load.
Jitter: Variation in delay that can disrupt real-time voice or video.
Roaming behavior: How representative clients transition between access points.
Interference: Competing radio energy or neighboring networks.
Client density: Simultaneous demand per access point and radio.
Optimization workflow
Establish baseline measurements.
Review coverage and RF conditions.
Analyze channels.
Review capacity and client load.
Approve configuration changes.
Repeat post-change tests.
Document results and remaining constraints.
Why is a speed test not enough? It measures one path at one moment. Signal, contention, density, roaming or upstream configuration can still make business Wi-Fi unreliable.
Will we need new access points? Not automatically. We compare placement, firmware support, load and client behavior before recommending reuse, relocation or replacement.
How do you measure Wi-Fi performance? Compare RSSI/SNR, utilization, packet loss, latency, jitter and throughput at agreed locations, then repeat after a controlled change.
Does optimization include monitoring forever? No. Ongoing monitoring, service hours and response targets belong in a separately agreed support plan.
Network baseline and change-record artifact: A planning example for recording location, load and repeatable tests; no measured customer performance result is asserted. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/guides/business-network-review/

title: A support plan tied to your actual equipment.
content:
KDH supports business routers, switches and Wi-Fi in Long Island and NYC through an agreed device inventory, diagnostic access and incident process. Support covers defined connectivity and configuration work; service hours and response targets are set in the contract.
Triage the reported issue: Record affected users, locations, devices, applications and start time. Compare wired and wireless access and check whether the issue follows one client, an access point, a VLAN or the ISP path.
Inspect logs and configuration: Review router and switch status, wireless client load, DNS/DHCP leases, VLAN routing and ISP/failover behavior where access is available. Preserve configuration before approved changes and agree on a maintenance window.
Verify and record the change: Test connectivity from the affected network segment and repeat the original user task. Document the cause, configuration change, remaining dependency and next action; escalate an ISP or hardware issue to its owner.
Is the issue wired, wireless or both?
Does DNS fail while direct connectivity works?
Is one VLAN unable to reach an approved resource?
Did the ISP failover trigger and restore as intended?
Can existing hardware be maintained, or has it reached a support limit?
Intermittent Wi-Fi, poor roaming, an overloaded access point, DNS failures, switch configuration errors, VLAN routing problems and connectivity loss require different checks. A device list and known network paths make those checks possible.
Deliverables:
Supported-device inventory, configuration access and dependency list
Agreed monitoring checks, service hours and incident contacts
Configuration/change notes and connectivity verification
ISP/vendor escalation notes and separately scoped improvement recommendations
Scope:
24/7 support applies only if explicitly contracted. Replacement hardware and ISP fees are separate; cabling projects need a separate scope. Cybersecurity/SOC services are separate unless included. Third-party vendor SLAs are not controlled by KDH. Support does not guarantee uptime or resolution before a vendor restores service.
Pricing basis:
Published Network monthly support is $200, $350 or $600 for the corresponding package scope. Onboarding, device count, sites, management access, monitoring and service hours affect the proposal. The setup ranges below describe network projects, not a support-only onboarding fee.
Incident workflow
Receive an alert or reported issue.
Triage the impact and affected users.
Identify the device or network path.
Review logs and configuration.
Approve and perform remediation.
Test connectivity and the original task.
Document the change, result and remaining dependencies.
When support needs a separate project
A failed switch and an office-wide coverage problem need different scopes. Routine support can isolate the issue; a new wireless design, replacement equipment rollout or cabling change needs an approved project. A configuration change cannot overcome an ISP outage or a physical coverage constraint.
Do you offer 24/7 support? Only where explicitly contracted. Confirm coverage hours, response targets and escalation contacts in the support agreement.
Does support include new hardware? Replacement hardware, ISP fees and cabling projects are separate unless the proposal expressly includes them.
Can we keep existing equipment? We review support status, firmware, access and capacity before recommending reuse or replacement.
What should we send with an incident? Send the affected location, device, connection type, application and time through the agreed support channel. Never send credentials in a general inquiry.
Example network planning artifact: An illustrative segmentation and incident-record checklist, not a claimed customer network or uptime result. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/guides/business-network-review/#network-example

title: Connect useful content to a measurable next step.
content:
We review crawlability, metadata, service content, internal links, and consent-aware measurement. Search rankings, AI citations, and commercial results are evaluated over time and are not guaranteed.
Search Console opportunity analysis: Review query/page pairs, impressions, clicks and comparable reporting periods. Separate a visibility gap from a page that receives visits but does not explain the offer or complete an inquiry.
Query-to-page intent mapping: Map each meaningful buyer query to the page that answers it. Identify competing pages and missing service detail before expanding content. Do not create near-duplicate city pages.
Crawl and indexability review: Check status codes, robots directives, sitemap eligibility, canonicals and rendered text. A valid sitemap does not guarantee indexing; inspect actual Search Console coverage.
Landing-page optimization: Review the service answer, buyer questions, proof, mobile CTA and form friction. Keep a relevant page useful before chasing more visits.
Internal linking: Connect service pages to related services, substantive guides and appropriately attributed work. Use descriptive links to explain the next decision.
Technical SEO: Inspect heading semantics, metadata, structured data and performance regressions. Prioritize issues that block discovery or interrupt a key task instead of promising speed will produce rankings.
Local entity consistency: Review business name, contact details, actual Freeport base and service-area wording across approved profiles. Do not invent offices, reviews or local credentials.
Conversion measurement: Review GA4, Google Tag Manager (GTM) where used, consent behavior and Search Console access. Test CTA engagement separately from server-confirmed form delivery or CRM acceptance. Qualification and revenue require business follow-up.
Digital authority and relevant link acquisition: Identify useful original resources and relevant editorial opportunities. Record outreach scope and publisher decisions; do not sell guaranteed placements or bulk link counts.
AI citation monitoring: Agree on a fixed set of buyer prompts and engines. Record the answer, citation and date, then compare repeat runs without treating one response as a permanent position.
Are the right queries finding the intended landing page?
Can a mobile visitor understand the service and reach the CTA?
Does a form submission or assistant handoff actually arrive?
Which delivered inquiries become qualified leads, meetings and clients?
What can we verify without promising a ranking or citation?
Traffic alone does not explain whether people can find your services or become customers. We review technical search foundations, service content, internal links, and inquiry measurement so you can see where the funnel needs work.
Deliverables:
A technical and content audit with prioritized actions
Agreed improvements to metadata, indexing, internal links, and service content
Consent-aware conversion measurement and a reporting framework tied to inquiries
Scope:
Search rankings, inclusion in AI answers, and inquiry volumes are not guaranteed. Media spend, paid campaign management, large content programs, and social publishing require an explicit scope. Account access and historical Search Console and GA4 data are dependencies.
Pricing basis:
SEO setup is part of the relevant published Web package scope. Ongoing marketing work depends on the audit, pages, content production, and reporting cadence; a support price is not an unlimited marketing retainer.
What the metrics mean
Impression: A search engine displayed the page.
Click: A searcher visited the site; not a qualified opportunity.
CTA engagement: A visitor interacted with a next step; delivery is not yet confirmed.
Successful lead: The form or assistant successfully delivered the inquiry.
Qualified lead: The business confirmed a real opportunity.
Booked meeting: The prospect scheduled an appointment; an inquiry alone does not establish this.
Client: A revenue outcome confirmed by the business.
GEO and AI search: compare a fixed benchmark
AI visibility is not a single permanent ranking. Citations vary by prompt, engine and time. We propose a fixed prompt benchmark with the engine, date, answer and cited URL recorded for each run, then compare the same questions over time.
Crawlable service content, clear entities, contextual internal links and conventional technical SEO remain the foundation. Original evidence and relevant third-party authority can strengthen citation potential; neither a prompt test nor schema guarantees inclusion.
What KDH does not promise
No number-one ranking or guaranteed traffic.
No guaranteed leads or sales.
No guaranteed AI citations.
No guaranteed backlink placement. Relevant link acquisition depends on editorial fit and the publisher.
Do you guarantee a first-page ranking? No. Search platforms decide what to index and show. We focus on useful content and technical foundations that can be reviewed.
How do you measure success? Review search impressions and clicks, then confirmed inquiries, qualified conversations, consultations, proposals, and revenue. Keep engagement separate from leads.
Can you optimize for AI search? We apply conventional SEO: accessible text, internal links, accurate metadata, and structured data that matches visible content. Inclusion in AI answers is not guaranteed.
Do I need paid ads? Not necessarily. We first assess whether organic demand and the existing website support your goals. Paid campaigns are a separate decision and scope.
When should we review progress? Review the funnel weekly and compare 28-day search periods. Evaluate inquiry quality and commercial outcomes after 60–90 days before expanding content.
KDH measurement planning example: A proposed search-to-inquiry reporting artifact. It illustrates methodology, not a measured ranking, traffic or revenue result. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/guides/search-and-lead-measurement/
Jarvis inquiry handoff example: The implementation distinguishes engagement from confirmed CRM acceptance; it does not establish acquisition lift. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/ai-group/solutions/ai-lead-assistant/

title: Keep your website useful after launch.
content:
Start with an access and dependency review, then agree on maintenance, content changes, monitoring, and service hours. New features and emergency work are assessed separately.
Review access and dependencies: Inventory the framework/CMS, hosting, repositories, plugins, integrations, licenses and account owners. Record existing issues and who controls backups and restore access before confirming a plan.
Agree a measurable maintenance checklist: Choose availability, form, error, dependency and content checks within the plan. Define cadence, service hours, response targets and the channel for reporting incidents.
Make controlled updates: Review package/plugin changes for compatibility, approve content edits, preserve a rollback path and test the affected workflow. Larger features, migrations and redesigns require a separate project.
Verify delivery and document changes: Check the agreed inquiry path after changes, including server-confirmed delivery and integration failure states. Record what changed, the result and any provider dependency that remains open.
Who owns hosting, licenses, backups and restore access?
Which pages, forms and integrations are checked, and how often?
What service hours and response targets apply?
Which content edits are included, and who approves them?
When does a request become a separate project or emergency scope?
Broken forms, outdated content, plugin changes, and slow pages can interrupt the customer journey. We start with an audit and agree on routine maintenance, update priorities, and a process for reporting issues.
Deliverables:
An agreed maintenance scope and access inventory
Scheduled updates, content changes, or performance work within the selected plan
Checks of key inquiry paths, reporting, and handoff notes for changes
Scope:
Response times, service hours, backups, and monitoring must be agreed in writing. Support does not promise uninterrupted uptime or unlimited development. Emergency recovery, major redesigns, hosting, licenses, and new integrations may require separate work.
Pricing basis:
Published Web support prices are $150, $250, and $500 per month for the corresponding package scope. Existing websites are assessed before recommending a plan. Setup totals below apply to website projects, not automatically to support-only work.
Operational support checklist
Availability: HTTP/endpoint checks at an agreed cadence.
Forms: Safe test submission and verification of successful delivery.
Dependencies: Package/plugin update review, compatibility checks and rollback.
Performance: Core Web Vitals and asset regressions for agreed pages.
Content: Agreed updates, revision limits and approval.
Errors: Build, runtime and log review where access is available.
SEO: Indexability and broken-link checks where included.
Integrations: API/form/CRM health and failure states where included.
What requires separate project scope
A redesign or new feature development.
A major CMS migration or hosting/provider migration.
A new custom integration.
An emergency incident outside the plan.
Substantial content production.
Update cadence versus immediate change
Batching routine updates in a maintenance window allows compatibility checks and rollback preparation. An urgent failure needs its own triage path and agreed coverage; a monthly price alone does not imply immediate or 24/7 response.
Confirm backup ownership and restoration access before changing dependencies. Monitoring may detect an error, but provider access or a third-party outage can still limit remediation.
Can you support a site you did not build? We review its framework, hosting, dependencies, access, and existing issues before confirming scope.
Are content edits included? The plan defines the kinds and volume of edits included. Larger content changes and new features are estimated separately.
Is support available 24/7? Service hours, response targets, and any emergency arrangements must be explicitly agreed.
Will you check our contact form? Key inquiry paths can be included in the maintenance checklist with safe test procedures and delivery checks.
Can we add features later? Yes. We assess new features separately and agree on cost, schedule, and acceptance checks.
DermCare Management portfolio: Modular content and responsive templates illustrate a maintainable structure; no ongoing support contract or uptime result is asserted. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/case-studies/dermcare/

title: Leave with a decision, not an obligation to build.
content:
KDH helps Long Island and NYC businesses decide whether a repeated task needs AI, ordinary automation, or a simpler process. Consulting produces a decision and implementation scope; building and operating the system are separate engagements.
Map a single workflow: Bring a redacted example of the task, its frequency, the people involved, source documents, and the time spent today. We trace where information enters, which systems it crosses, and where a person checks the result.
Compare rules, retrieval and existing tools: A deterministic form, database query, integration, or rule-based workflow may be more reliable than adding an AI layer. We compare build versus buy, data access, operating effort, and the consequences of a wrong answer.
Define the smallest useful test: Agree on representative questions, expected sources or actions, human approvals, failure criteria, and usage assumptions. The recommendation identifies an MVP, integration dependencies, and what must be verified before a larger build.
What repeated task costs time today, and how often does it occur?
Where is the approved information, and who owns updates?
Could normal automation solve this more reliably?
What must never be automated, and who reviews the result?
What is the smallest useful version, and how will we evaluate it?
Repeated document search, inquiry routing, or copying data between systems can justify a review. A low-frequency task with clear rules may need a form or integration rather than a model.
Deliverables:
Workflow map and data-source inventory
Risk/approval matrix and integration map
MVP recommendation, build-versus-buy comparison and estimated implementation scope
Operating-cost assumptions and evaluation criteria
Scope:
Consulting does not include production development, data migration, ongoing support, or permission to use confidential records. Clinical diagnosis, autonomous care decisions, and other consequential approvals stay with qualified people. Any regulated-data workflow requires separately scoped review.
Pricing basis:
Consulting is scoped by workshops, source systems, workflow complexity, and decision artifacts. Published AI packages include consultation within their stated build scope; their setup totals are not a standalone consulting quote. Model usage, hosting and integration subscriptions remain separate.
The AI decision framework
Workflow: What repetitive task are we solving?
Frequency: How often does it occur?
Data: Where does source information live, and who approves it?
Rules: Could normal automation solve this more reliably?
Risk: What must never be automated?
Human review: Where must a person approve the result?
Integration: Which systems need to connect?
Cost: What does the manual workflow consume today?
MVP: What is the smallest useful version?
Measurement: How will success be evaluated?
Example workflows to assess, not claimed deployments
Healthcare: administrative intake, prior-authorization workflow support, FAQ assistance, knowledge retrieval and internal document search. No clinical diagnosis or autonomous care decisions.
Manufacturing: product discovery, quote qualification, documentation search and sales knowledge retrieval.
Professional services: lead qualification, document retrieval, an internal knowledge assistant and CRM workflow support.
Real estate: inquiry routing, property FAQs, CRM enrichment and internal document search.
Will you recommend against AI? Yes. If a form, query, existing tool, or rules-based integration meets the requirement more reliably, that is the recommendation.
How is consulting different from development? Consulting defines fit, risk, scope and evaluation. AI Development implements and tests an agreed workflow; deployment and support need their own scope.
What should we bring? Bring redacted task examples, current systems, source owners, frequency, manual effort, and the decisions that require approval.
Can we use our current software? We review supported APIs, permissions, licensing and export limits before suggesting a new tool or custom build.
Jarvis: the KDH working assistant: A repository-backed retrieval and inquiry-handoff demonstration, not evidence of revenue lift or a customer deployment. https://kingdomdesignhouse.com/ai-group/solutions/ai-lead-assistant/

title: Start with a business task, then choose the AI.
content:
Define the knowledge sources, permissions, integration requirements, representative test questions, and a human fallback. Retrieval and generated answers still require review; ongoing usage and evaluation are part of the operating plan.
Define one useful task: Map the source information, user permissions, supported actions and systems to connect. Compare a fixed form or rule-based workflow before committing to a custom assistant.
Build retrieval around approved knowledge: For RAG, index approved sources and preserve useful source references and permissions. Review chunks and search results separately from the generated answer. A source match is not proof that every generated claim is correct.
Evaluate before release: Use representative questions, expected sources, human ratings and failure classes. Test no retrieval, stale documents, unsupported actions, incomplete output, refusals and integration outages as well as routine questions.
Integrate with an explicit fallback: Scope CRM field mapping, allowed actions, retries and confirmation states. Define a human handoff and document usage costs, source ownership and regression checks for future model or configuration changes.
Which sources are approved, current and accessible to this user?
Which actions are permitted, and which require a person?
How do we recognize a correct answer and supported citation?
What happens with no source, conflicting information or a failed tool?
Who receives escalations and owns updates after launch?
When staff repeatedly answer the same questions or transfer information between tools, an assistant may help. We scope the knowledge sources, actions, permissions, handoff, and failure cases before building a prototype.
Deliverables:
A workflow map, approved knowledge sources, and success and failure criteria
A prototype assistant or integration with scoped permissions and a human fallback
Evaluation examples, integration checks, deployment notes, and an update process
Scope:
AI responses can be incomplete or incorrect. Human review is required for consequential decisions. Model usage, hosting, vector storage, external licenses, data cleanup, and ongoing evaluation are scoped separately. Do not use the public demo for sensitive records or patient information.
Pricing basis:
Published AI setup totals start at $4,000 with support from $300 per month. The final scope depends on retrieval sources, integrations, actions, evaluation, and operating requirements. Third-party usage charges are separate and vary with traffic and configuration.
Evaluation workflow
Choose a representative question, including out-of-scope requests.
Record the expected approved source.
Inspect retrieved chunks and permissions.
Review the generated response.
Validate citations and claims against the source.
Collect a human rating using agreed criteria.
Classify the failure and rerun after an approved change.
Common failure cases
No relevant retrieval, or the wrong source ranks first.
A stale source wins over current material.
A user requests an unsupported action.
The CRM/API is unavailable or a tool call fails.
The model refuses the request.
The output is incomplete.
The answer conflicts with source material.
Human handoff is a defined workflow
Escalate missing or conflicting sources, uncertainty, unsupported actions and failed integrations. Transfer the question, relevant approved source references, failure category and only the contact/context the user has agreed to provide. Set the destination and review owner before launch.
Keep clinical, legal, financial and other consequential approvals with qualified people. The assistant must not silently expand its permissions or invent successful actions. Offer a visible route to a person and explain when delivery has not been confirmed.
Jarvis provides a Contact fallback and a structured HubSpot inquiry handoff. CRM acceptance is not a booked meeting or a guaranteed human response time. For a client workflow, agree on redacted failure logs, access controls, retention and who reviews failed automation.
Retrieval is not model training
RAG supplies retrieved context from approved sources at answer time; it does not by itself train model weights on those documents. Retrieval can miss context and generated answers can still be wrong. Confirm provider data-handling terms separately for the selected deployment.
Start with the smallest useful source set and allowed action. Adding sources or tools broadens coverage and also increases evaluation, permission and maintenance work.
How is a custom assistant different from a basic chatbot? A fixed flow suits predictable questions. A custom assistant can retrieve approved knowledge and connect to tools, but needs more evaluation, maintenance, and oversight.
Can it connect to our CRM? We scope supported APIs, field mapping, permissions, retries, and failure handling. Jarvis has an implemented HubSpot handoff; your integration requires its own scope and verification.
Will it always answer correctly? No. We test representative questions, provide a human fallback, and define tasks the assistant must not perform.
What costs continue after launch? Support, model usage, hosting, retrieval storage, integration subscriptions, and content updates may continue. We identify these in the proposal rather than promise a fixed usage bill.
Can I try an example? Use the Jarvis demo for business questions and avoid sensitive information. It is a working assistant and may create a follow-up inquiry if you provide project and contact details.

title: An update process for an assistant already in use.
content:
KDH reviews production assistants for retrieval quality, unsupported answers, response time, usage cost and integration failures. We agree on monitoring access, test questions, review cadence and escalation responsibilities before taking on an existing system.
Establish an evaluation baseline: Collect representative questions with expected answers and approved sources. Include questions the assistant should decline or escalate. Review retrieval and generated output separately so a content issue is not mistaken for a model issue.
Classify before changing: An outdated document needs an approved knowledge refresh. A wrong retrieved source may need indexing or ranking changes. A failed CRM action needs integration diagnosis. We record the failure class, proposed change and acceptance check.
Retest and document: Run the representative set after source, prompt, model or integration changes. Compare source support, latency and usage against the baseline, obtain human review, and keep change notes and a rollback path. Improvements are evaluated, not automatic.
Did retrieval return the right approved source?
Does the answer add claims the source does not support?
Did an API, CRM action or tool call fail?
Did a provider or model change alter behavior?
Who approves the correction and checks the result?
An assistant can cite an outdated policy, retrieve the wrong document, or lose access to a CRM. Support starts by making those failures visible and defining who handles them.
Deliverables:
Access and dependency inventory with agreed monitoring signals
Representative test set and issue classification log
Approved content/configuration changes with regression checks
Change notes, escalation responsibilities and usage review
Scope:
The plan defines supported systems, review cadence, service hours and response targets. New tools, major integrations, fine-tuning, retraining and substantial data cleanup require separate scope. Provider outages and third-party SLAs are outside KDH control. No automatic accuracy improvement or uninterrupted availability is promised.
Pricing basis:
Published AI monthly support is $300, $500 or $800 within the corresponding package scope. An inherited assistant needs an access and dependency review first. Test-set size, knowledge changes, integrations and review cadence affect scope; provider usage, hosting and storage are separate.
How an AI assistant gets updated
Knowledge refresh: Approved documents or database content change.
Embedding refresh: New or changed material is re-indexed for search.
Retrieval tuning: Search, filters or ranking logic changes.
Prompt/configuration update: Behavior instructions or settings change.
Model change: A provider or model version changes; regression testing is needed.
Fine-tuning: Training examples adjust model behavior; not routine source maintenance.
Retraining: A significantly different training activity, not the default maintenance process for most KDH RAG-style systems.
The evaluation loop
Choose a representative test set.
Record the expected answer and approved source.
Inspect the retrieval result.
Inspect the generated answer.
Verify claims against the source.
Have a person review the result.
Classify the issue.
Approve a configuration or content update, then rerun the test set.
Common production failure modes
An outdated source wins over a current policy.
Retrieval returns the wrong policy or no relevant source.
The model generates an unsupported answer.
A CRM/API integration is unavailable or a tool call fails.
Token usage spikes and changes operating cost.
A user requests an unsupported action.
A provider change alters answer behavior.
Does adding documents retrain the model? No. Refreshing knowledge and embeddings changes what retrieval can find. Model training changes model behavior or weights and is a different activity.
Will the assistant improve on its own? No. Changes need an approved source or configuration update, evaluation and human review. Monitoring alone does not improve accuracy.
Can you support an assistant built elsewhere? We first review source ownership, logs, provider access, integrations and deployment documentation before confirming support scope.
Are new features included? Routine work follows the agreed plan. New actions, integrations or major changes need a separate estimate and acceptance checks.

title: Custom AI Assistant vs Chatbot: Fit, Costs & Maintenance
content:
The labels overlap: many products called chatbots already use generative AI. A more useful comparison is a fixed flow or FAQ tool versus an assistant that retrieves business knowledge and can connect to other systems. Choose based on the task, information, operating cost, and review your team can support.
When a simpler flow is enough
A short FAQ, service selector, or structured inquiry form can be easier to operate than an open-ended assistant. If every visitor needs the same few choices, define those choices clearly and provide a person to contact when the flow does not fit.
When retrieval and integration add value
A custom assistant may be useful when visitors ask varied questions across approved information or staff need a specific workflow spanning tools. Start with a narrow task and representative test questions. An assistant still needs accurate sources and explicit rules for what it may do.
Compare the full cost of operation
Compare implementation effort, subscription and usage charges, hosting, storage, integration licenses, support, and the time people spend maintaining and reviewing the system. Avoid choosing based only on the demo or setup price.
KDH publishes AI setup totals from $4,000 and support from $300 per month. These are package starting points, not a guaranteed total operating bill. A simpler existing tool may be more appropriate for a small, fixed task.
Decide how a person takes over
Define a clear handoff for uncertainty, missing information, and integration failure. Keep consequential decisions with people, restrict actions, and avoid collecting sensitive records in a public business demo.
Jarvis demonstrates service questions and an implemented HubSpot inquiry handoff. Opening it is engagement; successful CRM acceptance or Contact notification delivery is the point at which KDH records an inquiry.
Is an AI assistant always better? No. A fixed flow or ordinary form may solve the problem with less cost and maintenance.
Can an assistant make mistakes with approved sources? Yes. Retrieval can miss context and generated answers can be incorrect. Use evaluation questions, clear limitations, and human escalation.
What should I prepare before choosing? List common questions, approved sources, systems involved, expected usage, who maintains the content, and the decisions a person must review.
Will either option increase sales? Neither guarantees sales. Measure confirmed inquiries and qualified commercial outcomes against a real baseline.

title: Business Network Review: Devices, Segmentation & Incidents
content:
Bring the current device inventory, building layout, ISP details and a record of the failing task. This checklist helps distinguish incident support, performance tuning and a new network design.
Record what exists
List routers, switches, access points, firmware and management owners. Record uplinks, VLANs, IP ranges, DHCP/DNS services, ISP handoffs and any secondary connection. Keep credentials in an approved secure channel, not a public inquiry.
Mark user locations, walls, cabling, PoE requirements and latency-sensitive voice or video applications. Record where and when a problem occurs, then compare a wired client with Wi-Fi at the same time.
Example small-business network architecture
Internet / ISP → Firewall / Gateway → Core switch → Wireless access points and wired clients. Example segments: VLAN 10 — Staff; VLAN 20 — Voice; VLAN 30 — Guest; VLAN 40 — IoT.
This is an example only, not a customer installation. Actual segmentation depends on devices, business requirements, risk, building layout and existing systems. VLANs require explicit routing/firewall rules; assigning a VLAN number alone does not enforce isolation.
Design checks include uplink capacity, switch ports and PoE budget, guest isolation, approved inter-VLAN paths, device management access and failover behavior. Dual ISPs can still share a physical failure point.
Keep a useful incident record
Record the time, affected device and location, original task, network path, observed signal or connectivity result, and relevant log reference. Distinguish an ISP problem from a client, access-point or configuration issue.
For a change, retain the previous configuration, approval, maintenance window, rollback plan and post-change connectivity check. This is a proposed documentation format, not an uptime or response-time commitment.
Compare a baseline with the same test
Review RSSI and SNR for coverage, channel utilization for contention, and packet loss, latency, jitter and throughput for the affected application. Repeat tests at the same locations and comparable client load.
A speed test is one path at one moment. It does not establish roaming quality or coverage across a building. Optimization may help existing equipment; physical coverage, cabling or hardware limits can require a separately scoped design.
Must we buy new access points? Not automatically. Confirm firmware support, capacity, placement, management access and cabling before recommending replacement.
Does this checklist include a security assessment? No. Cybersecurity/SOC work and regulated requirements require explicit specialist scope.
What should we measure first? Record the original failing task and location, compare wired and wireless paths, then choose measurements that test the suspected cause.
Network design decisions: Use the illustrative architecture to prepare requirements, not as proof of a particular deployment.

title: Search Traffic, Delivered Inquiries & Qualified Leads
content:
A useful report records where a prospect entered, whether the inquiry arrived and what the business did next. More clicks alone do not establish more qualified leads. This is a measurement framework, not a claim of measured campaign results.
Map the query to the page
Export Search Console query/page pairs for comparable periods. Identify queries with relevant intent, the pages shown and whether multiple pages compete for the same task. Record impressions and clicks separately from inquiry behavior.
Inspect crawlability, canonicals, metadata and visible service answers before expanding content. Prioritize the page that can answer the buyer question with evidence and a clear next step.
Treat delivery as a distinct event
In this repository, a CTA click, chat opening or chat message is engagement. A form is recorded as an inquiry only after the server confirms notification delivery; a Jarvis handoff requires confirmed CRM acceptance. Opening the assistant does not book a meeting.
Review GA4 and any GTM configuration with consent rules. Keep personal information and transcripts out of analytics payloads. Test failed submissions and failed integrations as well as success; a button click must not become a delivered lead.
Use a business-reviewed funnel
Track impression → click → CTA engagement → successful lead → qualified lead → booked meeting → client. Keep a record of the stage definition, source of confirmation and owner for each stage.
Qualification, scheduling and revenue need business follow-up. Compare source, inquiry quality and actual opportunities rather than treating every delivered request as a sale. Consent and missing attribution can leave gaps; label them instead of inventing a source.
Benchmark AI citations consistently
Choose fixed buyer prompts, record the engine, date, answer and cited URL, and repeat the same set. Results vary across prompts, engines and time; one answer does not establish a permanent AI ranking.
Useful original evidence, relevant third-party authority and conventional SEO can support discoverability. There is no guarantee of a ranking, traffic, leads, AI citation or backlink placement.
Is a CTA click a lead? No. It indicates engagement. Confirm successful delivery before counting an inquiry.
How long does SEO take? There is no fixed result deadline. Review comparable search periods and delivered inquiry quality; timing depends on indexing, demand, site changes and competition.
Can AI citations be guaranteed? No. Benchmark the same prompts and engines over time, and record the observed citations without promising future inclusion.

title: Website & Application Planning: Scope, Ownership & Failure
content:
Before a redesign or application build, record who uses the system, what they need to do, which content works today and what happens when a dependency fails. This is a project planning artifact, not a customer result.
Inventory the existing journey
List current URLs, useful content, top landing pages, navigation, forms and known delivery issues. Map the visitor’s task from search intent to service answer, relevant proof and inquiry. Preserve useful URLs and brand assets when they still serve that task.
On mobile, check whether the offer and next step are understandable, the form requests appropriate information, and a successful submission actually arrives. Distinguish visual friction from an integration failure.
Choose rendering and data ownership
Stable public content may suit static generation; frequently changing or personalized data may require server rendering or an authenticated application request. Define freshness and access requirements before selecting an architecture.
Agree what editors manage in the CMS and what transactional state belongs in an application database. Record account ownership, roles, licenses, migration volumes and handoff access. A brochure website package does not include an unlimited custom application.
Plan an integration failure before launch
For each API, record the data fields, allowed actions, timeout, retry limit and owner. Identify actions that must be idempotent so a retry or duplicate webhook cannot repeat a transaction.
For form notifications and CRM handoffs, define confirmation and failure states. A button click is engagement, not proof of delivery. Agree how a user retries, reaches a person or learns that the action failed.
Separate launch from ongoing operation
Agree on acceptance checks for core workflows, permissions, migration and release rollback. Document deployment access, cache invalidation, backup/restore ownership and the previous working version.
State whether hosting, licenses, content production, routine support and emergency recovery are included. Template count, integrations, data cleanup, roles and testing drive cost; commercial results are not guaranteed.
Who owns the code? The proposal defines ownership and repository handoff; third-party software retains its license terms. Agree on accounts and access before work starts.
Can we retain our current CMS? Review supported templates, APIs, access, content and migration constraints before choosing extension or replacement.
Is support included with a build? Confirm the plan, service hours, checks and exclusions separately. A launch does not imply unlimited ongoing development.
